summary.text: A 67-year-old Caucasian woman with a body mass index of 30 was referred to clinic with symptoms of biliary colic. Her past history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, asthma and a previous total abdominal hysterectomy, and she was a nonsmoker with minimal alcohol intake. Abdominal examination was normal with no jaundice or anaemia. Ultrasound showed a 13 mm common bile duct containing a 12 mm stone, and liver function tests were reported.

She underwent ERCP with sphincterotomy, straight stent placement and removal of several stones, but one large stone could not be removed with the Dormia basket and was left in situ. At a repeat ERCP three weeks later the large common bile duct stone was engaged in a Dormia basket for mechanical lithotripsy, but on cranking the lithotripter handle the wires snapped externally at the mouth.

She was referred to upper gastrointestinal surgery and taken as an emergency to the operating theatre the same day. Following laparoscopic cholecystectomy, laparoscopic common bile duct exploration through a choledochotomy confirmed the impacted basket and stone, the stone was fragmented under direct vision, and most fragments were removed with a Fogarty catheter and second basket. The ERCP basket was then delivered into the duodenum and removed orally, clearance was confirmed and the choledochotomy was closed.
After ERCP she was readmitted with acute pancreatitis and was hospitalised for 10 days, following which she made a full recovery.

ambiguities.issue: The source says only "After ERCP" for the readmission with acute pancreatitis; it does not state whether this followed the first ERCP or the repeat ERCP, nor how the readmission relates to the surgical retrieval. Only the order after the first ERCP holds under either reading and is recorded.

ambiguities.issue: The case narrative locates the impacted basket and stone at the ampulla, the abstract in the common bile duct and the Figure 3 caption in the distal common bile duct; these are compatible descriptions of one site at different granularity, not two values. The Figure 1 caption places the gallstone near the top of the common bile duct at the earlier repeat ERCP. Each is recorded as stated.

The source gives no calendar dates, so every time is relative; the ERCP preceding the pancreatitis readmission is not identified.
Regular medications are listed without dose, route or indication; their action is recorded as unknown.
